items.stem: Define the term "barter".
items.answer: Exchanging goods or services directly for other goods or services without money
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: exchanging goods or services directly for other goods or services without money. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why money is more efficient than barter.
items.answer: Money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants, provides a common unit to compare values, is divisible and can be stored, making trade much easier.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants, provides a common unit to compare values, is divisible and can be stored, making trade much easier. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Banks keep all the money that people deposit in their vaults." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Banks keep only a small fraction as reserves and lend most deposits to borrowers.
items.markingKey: Banks keep only a small fraction as reserves and lend most deposits to borrowers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why credit can sometimes lead to a debt trap.
items.answer: If interest rates are high or income falls, for example after a crop failure, borrowers may be unable to repay and must borrow more, so debt grows.
items.markingKey: Content: If interest rates are high or income falls, for example after a crop failure, borrowers may be unable to repay and must borrow more, so debt grows. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.answer: It investigates the impact of a financial innovation on development.

items.answer: Read Suri and Jack (2016) and FinAccess survey data; compare urban and rural households; evaluate sources; cite in APA.

items.stem: Who controls the issue of currency notes in India?
items.answer: The Reserve Bank of India
items.markingKey: B. The RBI is India's central bank.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a central bank and a commercial bank.
items.answer: A central bank, such as the Reserve Bank of India, issues currency and regulates banks; a commercial bank takes deposits and lends to households and businesses for profit.
items.markingKey: A central bank, such as the Reserve Bank of India, issues currency and regulates banks; a commercial bank takes deposits and lends to households and businesses for profit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between informal credit and formal credit.
items.answer: Formal credit comes from banks and co-operatives regulated by the central bank, usually at lower interest; informal credit comes from moneylenders, traders or relatives, often at high interest and without regulation.
items.markingKey: Formal credit comes from banks and co-operatives regulated by the central bank, usually at lower interest; informal credit comes from moneylenders, traders or relatives, often at high interest and without regulation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source A – Nobel lecture (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Muhammad Yunus, Nobel Peace Prize lecture, Oslo, 10 December 2006

The speaker said that he had lent a small amount of his own money to 42 people in a village in 1976 to free them from moneylenders. He argued that poor people are creditworthy and that credit should be treated as a human right.

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: Poor people are creditworthy and credit can free them from moneylenders.
items.markingKey: Poor people are creditworthy and credit can free them from moneylenders. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: A traveller changes 400 euros into Swiss francs at a rate of 1 euro = 0.95 Swiss francs. How much do they receive?
items.answer: 380.00 Swiss francs

items.stem: Lukas can save €1,000 for 6 years in Account A (3% simple interest) or Account B (3% interest compounded annually). Calculate the interest earned in each account and explain why they differ.
items.markingKey: A: 1,000 × 0.03 × 6 = €180.00 (A1). B: 1,000 × (1 + 0.03)^6 − 1,000 = €194.05 (M1 A1). B earns more because interest is paid on previous interest (compounding) (R1).

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Microcredit is the most effective way to reduce poverty." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Microcredit helps some households but is not a cure-all; it works best alongside savings, insurance, education and wider development.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it gives poor people, especially women, access to capital without collateral; Grameen and others have reached millions of borrowers. Counter-arguments: randomised studies found modest average effects on income; high interest rates and over-indebtedness have caused crises, as in Andhra Pradesh in 2010. Thesis/conclusion: Microcredit helps some households but is not a cure-all; it works best alongside savings, insurance, education and wider development. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Which country was the world's largest exporter of goods in the 2020s?
items.answer: China
items.markingKey: D. It exported about US$ 3.4 trillion of goods in 2023.

items.stem: Explain why trade can benefit consumers.
items.answer: Consumers gain access to a wider choice of goods, often at lower prices, and competition from imports encourages domestic firms to improve quality.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Consumers gain access to a wider choice of goods, often at lower prices, and competition from imports encourages domestic firms to improve quality. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Trade only benefits the country with the absolute advantage." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Both trading partners can gain if they specialise according to comparative advantage.
items.markingKey: Both trading partners can gain if they specialise according to comparative advantage. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: India's exports of services went from 52 US$ billion in 2005 to 340 US$ billion in 2023. Which is the percentage change?

Source A – Economics text (paraphrased): Paraphrase of David Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, London, 1817

The author argued that England and Portugal would both gain if England specialised in cloth and Portugal in wine and they traded, even though Portugal could produce both goods with less labour than England.

According to Source A, what can we learn about why countries trade: imports, exports and specialisation? Support your answer with details from the source.
items.answer: Both countries gain from specialising according to comparative advantage.
items.markingKey: Both countries gain from specialising according to comparative advantage. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Free trade benefits all countries equally."
items.answer: Thesis: Trade raises overall welfare, but gains are not equal; policies such as support for affected workers and diversification help spread the benefits.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: trade raises total output and gives consumers cheaper goods; export-led growth helped East Asian economies develop. Counter-arguments: gains are unequal; some industries and workers lose; countries exporting raw materials may face falling prices and dependency. Thesis/conclusion: Trade raises overall welfare, but gains are not equal; policies such as support for affected workers and diversification help spread the benefits. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "absolute advantage".
items.answer: The ability of a country to produce more of a good than another country with the same resources
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the ability of a country to produce more of a good than another country with the same resources. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between absolute advantage and comparative advantage.
items.answer: Absolute advantage means producing more with the same resources; comparative advantage means producing at a lower opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: Absolute advantage means producing more with the same resources; comparative advantage means producing at a lower opportunity cost. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Supply-chain studies suggest coffee farmers receive about 1.5% of the US$ 3.20 price of a cup of coffee in a café. A fair-trade scheme raises the amount they receive per cup by 5%, with the rest of the price unchanged. Calculate their new payment per unit and the new retail price, and evaluate whether this would make a large difference to consumers.
items.answer: US$ 0.050 per cup; new price US$ 3.202
items.markingKey: Current payment 1.5% × 3.20 = US$ 0.0480 (M1); × 1.05 = US$ 0.0504 (A1); extra US$ 0.0024, so new price US$ 3.2024 (M1 A1). Evaluation (R1): the price rise is tiny for consumers, but a significant gain for producers; however only part of output may sell on fair-trade terms.

items.stem: "Buying fair-trade products is the most effective way consumers can help producers in developing countries." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Fair trade helps some producers and raises awareness, but systemic changes in trade and corporate behaviour are needed for wider impact.

Source A – Economics text (paraphrased): Paraphrase of David Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, London, 1817

The author argued that England and Portugal would both gain if England specialised in cloth and Portugal in wine and they traded, even though Portugal could produce both goods with less labour than England.

"Free trade benefits all countries equally." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Trade raises overall welfare, but gains are not equal; policies such as support for affected workers and diversification help spread the benefits.
items.markingKey: From the source: Both countries gain from specialising according to comparative advantage. Own knowledge for: trade raises total output and gives consumers cheaper goods; export-led growth helped East Asian economies develop. Own knowledge against: gains are unequal; some industries and workers lose; countries exporting raw materials may face falling prices and dependency. Judgement: Trade raises overall welfare, but gains are not equal; policies such as support for affected workers and diversification help spread the benefits. items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Buying fair-trade products is the most effective way consumers can help producers in developing countries." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Fair trade helps some producers and raises awareness, but systemic changes in trade and corporate behaviour are needed for wider impact.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it guarantees minimum prices and funds community projects; it raises awareness of supply-chain inequality. Counter-arguments: only a small share of trade is certified and benefits are uneven; changes in trade rules, wages and corporate practice may have bigger effects. Thesis/conclusion: Fair trade helps some producers and raises awareness, but systemic changes in trade and corporate behaviour are needed for wider impact. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem:
Source A – Nobel lecture (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Muhammad Yunus, Nobel Peace Prize lecture, Oslo, 10 December 2006

The speaker said that he had lent a small amount of his own money to 42 people in a village in 1976 to free them from moneylenders. He argued that poor people are creditworthy and that credit should be treated as a human right.

"Microcredit is the most effective way to reduce poverty." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Microcredit helps some households but is not a cure-all; it works best alongside savings, insurance, education and wider development.
items.markingKey: From the source: Poor people are creditworthy and credit can free them from moneylenders. Own knowledge for: it gives poor people, especially women, access to capital without collateral; Grameen and others have reached millions of borrowers. Own knowledge against: randomised studies found modest average effects on income; high interest rates and over-indebtedness have caused crises, as in Andhra Pradesh in 2010. Judgement: Microcredit helps some households but is not a cure-all; it works best alongside savings, insurance, education and wider development. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. items.stem: With the same resources, Brazil can produce 100 units of rice or 20 units of electronics; Germany can produce 50 units of rice or 160 units of electronics. Calculate the opportunity cost of one unit of rice in each country and state which good each should specialise in.
items.answer: Brazil: 0.2 electronics; Germany: 3.2 electronics; Brazil → rice, Germany → electronics
items.markingKey: Brazil: 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2 units of electronics per rice (A1); Germany: 160 ÷ 50 = 3.2 (A1). Lower opportunity cost of rice in Brazil → comparative advantage in rice; Germany in electronics (R1 R1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "barter"?
options: The function of money that allows wealth to be saved for future use
An arrangement to borrow money or obtain goods now and pay later, usually with interest
An asset, such as land or a house, that a borrower pledges to a lender as security for a loan
Exchanging goods or services directly for other goods or services without money
items.answer: Exchanging goods or services directly for other goods or services without money
items.markingKey: D. "barter" is exchanging goods or services directly for other goods or services without money.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "absolute advantage"?
options: A good or service sold to another country
The function of money that allows wealth to be saved for future use
The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
The ability of a country to produce more of a good than another country with the same resources
items.answer: The ability of a country to produce more of a good than another country with the same resources
items.markingKey: D. "absolute advantage" is the ability of a country to produce more of a good than another country with the same resources.

items.stem: Which 2013 factory collapse in Bangladesh, killing over 1,100 garment workers, increased pressure for ethical clothing?
items.answer: Rana Plaza
items.markingKey: Rana Plaza. It led to the Bangladesh Accord on building safety.

items.stem: A student claims: "Banks keep all the money that people deposit in their vaults." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Banks keep only a small fraction as reserves and lend most deposits to borrowers.
items.markingKey: Banks keep only a small fraction as reserves and lend most deposits to borrowers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between comparative advantage and absolute advantage.
items.answer: Absolute advantage means producing more with the same resources; comparative advantage means producing at a lower opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: Absolute advantage means producing more with the same resources; comparative advantage means producing at a lower opportunity cost. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why producers of crops like coffee need a minimum price.
items.answer: World prices for commodities can fall sharply because of oversupply or speculation, so a guaranteed minimum protects farmers' incomes from collapse.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: World prices for commodities can fall sharply because of oversupply or speculation, so a guaranteed minimum protects farmers' incomes from collapse. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between formal credit and informal credit.
items.answer: Formal credit comes from banks and co-operatives regulated by the central bank, usually at lower interest; informal credit comes from moneylenders, traders or relatives, often at high interest and without regulation.
items.markingKey: Formal credit comes from banks and co-operatives regulated by the central bank, usually at lower interest; informal credit comes from moneylenders, traders or relatives, often at high interest and without regulation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why governments sometimes impose tariffs.
items.answer: Tariffs protect domestic industries and jobs from foreign competition, raise revenue and may be used in trade disputes, though they raise prices for consumers.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Tariffs protect domestic industries and jobs from foreign competition, raise revenue and may be used in trade disputes, though they raise prices for consumers. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Hana writes: "Fairtrade guarantees that all farmers escape poverty." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Studies show mixed results: Fairtrade can stabilise incomes, but many certified farmers remain poor because only part of their crop sells on Fairtrade terms.
items.markingKey: Studies show mixed results: Fairtrade can stabilise incomes, but many certified farmers remain poor because only part of their crop sells on Fairtrade terms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into the functions of money and the role of banks and credit?
options: How has M-Pesa affected the savings of rural households in Kenya since 2007?
items.answer: How has M-Pesa affected the savings of rural households in Kenya since 2007?
items.markingKey: A. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

Source A – Economics text (paraphrased): Paraphrase of David Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, London, 1817

The author argued that England and Portugal would both gain if England specialised in cloth and Portugal in wine and they traded, even though Portugal could produce both goods with less labour than England.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching why countries trade: imports, exports and specialisation? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of David Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, London, 1817. Purpose: to argue against protectionist laws such as the Corn Laws. Value: It is the founding statement of comparative advantage, explained with a clear example. Limitation: It is a simplified model that assumes full employment, no transport costs and no change in technology.

items.stem: Using Kuapa Kokoo in Ghana as an example, explain fair trade and co-operatives.
items.answer: A cocoa co-operative founded in 1993 with around 100,000 members; it co-owns the Divine Chocolate company and uses Fairtrade premiums for wells and schools. Farmers gained a share of profits further up the supply chain.

items.stem: In one year a country such as Sri Lanka exported goods worth US$ 5.5 billion and imported goods worth US$ 8.1 billion. Calculate its balance of trade in goods and state whether it is a surplus or a deficit.
items.answer: US$ -2.6 billion (deficit)
items.markingKey: Balance of trade = exports − imports = 5.5 − 8.1 = -2.6 bn (M1 A1).
